output.query: arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy diagnostic criteria and ICD indications

results.finding: Criteria in six categories (global or regional RV dysfunction, tissue characterisation, repolarisation, depolarisation, arrhythmias, family history); a definite diagnosis needs two major, one major and two minor, or four minor criteria from different categories. T-wave inversion in V1-V3 without RBBB after age 14 and regional RV dyskinesia with RVEDV/BSA of 100 mL/m2 or more in women (or RVEF 40% or less) on MRI are major criteria.
results.source: Marcus FI et al., Diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy/dysplasia: proposed modification of the Task Force Criteria. Circulation 2010;121:1533-1541

results.finding: In ARVC, an ICD is recommended after haemodynamically poorly tolerated sustained VT and should be considered after arrhythmic syncope; beta-blockers and restriction of high-intensity exercise are advised, with genetic testing and cascade screening of first-degree relatives.
results.source: Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death. Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997-4126

output.summary: ARVC is diagnosed with the 2010 Task Force Criteria; ESC 2022 sets ICD indications by arrhythmic events and advises beta-blockers, exercise restriction and family screening.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: T-wave inversion V1-V3 without RBBB, possible epsilon wave in V1, PVCs of LBBB morphology with inferior axis
action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG on arrival
action_criteria.rationale: Exertional syncope with palpitations and a father who died suddenly at 44 is high risk; the ECG looks for repolarisation and depolarisation abnormalities and ventricular ectopy (ESC 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Supine 118/72 mmHg, HR 88; standing 3 min 114/75 mmHg, HR 94: no orthostatic hypotension
action_criteria.label: Orthostatic blood pressure by active standing (supine, then 1 and 3 minutes standing)
action_criteria.rationale: Orthostatic blood pressure on active standing is part of the initial evaluation of every transient loss of consciousness (ESC 2018 Class I); it tests orthostatic hypotension, the competing cause, before a cardiac cause is accepted.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Potassium 4.1 and creatinine 0.7 normal, magnesium 4.4 mg/dL on the infusion, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.18
action_criteria.label: Electrolytes, magnesium and urinalysis (BMP, magnesium, urinalysis)
action_criteria.rationale: Potassium and magnesium matter in ventricular arrhythmia and the empirical magnesium infusion needs a level; urine protein with renal function excludes the pre-eclampsia that the referral assumed (ESC 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mildly dilated RV with subtricuspid free-wall hypokinesis and TAPSE 18 mm; normal LV size, LVEF 58%
action_criteria.label: Transthoracic echocardiogram
action_criteria.rationale: Exertional syncope with ventricular ectopy needs structural assessment: the echo shows the RV abnormality and excludes peripartum cardiomyopathy (ESC 2018; ESC 2023).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Seven NSVT runs up to 12 beats at 185 bpm, two with symptoms; 4,832 PVCs (4.3%) of LBBB morphology
action_criteria.label: Inpatient telemetry
action_criteria.rationale: Exertional syncope with palpitations and a family history of sudden death is high risk: immediate in-hospital ECG monitoring is Class I and provides the symptom-rhythm correlation (ESC 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Subtricuspid RV free-wall dyskinesia, RVEDVI 112 mL/m2, RVEF 39%, RV fat and enhancement; normal LV
action_criteria.label: Cardiac MRI
action_criteria.rationale: The echo shows an RV abnormality without meeting the imaging criteria; cardiac MRI quantifies RV volume and function and regional wall motion for the 2010 Task Force Criteria (ESC 2023).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Exercise-induced NSVT of LBBB morphology with superior axis at peak exercise
action_criteria.label: Exercise stress test
action_criteria.rationale: Exercise testing can show exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmia, but telemetry has already captured symptomatic NSVT and testing 10 days after a caesarean section can be deferred (ESC 2022).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Heterozygous pathogenic PKP2 variant c.2013delC (p.Lys672Argfs*12), frameshift with predicted loss of function
action_criteria.label: Cardiomyopathy gene panel (desmosomal genes) with genetic counselling
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic counselling and testing are recommended in ARVC (ESC 2023 Class I): a pathogenic desmosomal variant is a major 2010 Task Force criterion and enables cascade testing, starting with the sister; it does not change the ICD decision, hence recommended.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Metoprolol or propranolol: low transfer into breast milk; possible extra hypotension with the infusion
action_criteria.label: Review the planned beta-blocker for breastfeeding and interactions
action_criteria.rationale: A beta-blocker is started in a breastfeeding mother; the review confirms low milk transfer and the interactions with the magnesium infusion and ibuprofen (LactMed; ESC 2022).

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose eclampsia or epilepsy and do not start antiseizure medication for the convulsive syncope
Do not discharge before ICD implantation
Do not choose atenolol, nadolol or sotalol while she is breastfeeding (high transfer into breast milk; LactMed)
Do not clear her to return to endurance or competitive exercise
required_recommendations: Diagnose arrhythmic syncope from ventricular tachycardia due to arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, definite by the 2010 Task Force Criteria (major: T-wave inversion V1-V3; major: regional RV dyskinesia with RVEDVI 112 mL/m2 and RVEF 39% on MRI), not eclampsia or epilepsy
Admit to a monitored bed with continuous ECG monitoring and a defibrillator available until an ICD is implanted
Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion: eclampsia is excluded (normal blood pressure, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.18, normal platelets and liver enzymes)
Implant an ICD before discharge (ESC 2022: should be considered after arrhythmic syncope in ARVC, here with NSVT and RV dysfunction)
Start a beta-blocker compatible with breastfeeding, metoprolol or propranolol (LactMed), titrated to heart rate and blood pressure
Advise against competitive and high-intensity endurance exercise for life (ESC 2022)
Offer genetic counselling and testing (desmosomal genes) with cascade clinical and genetic screening of first-degree relatives, starting with her sister who reports palpitations
Counsel on contraception and on the risk of a future pregnancy, with cardio-obstetric review before any further pregnancy
Advise no driving until 3 months after ICD implantation without arrhythmia recurrence (ESC 2018, Group 1)

differential.key_features: Referred as postpartum seizures, but blood pressure is 118-124 systolic, there is no headache or visual disturbance, the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 0.18, platelets and liver enzymes are normal, and telemetry captures symptomatic NSVT.
Ventricular arrhythmia 10 days postpartum raises it, but LVEF is 58% on echocardiography and 60% on MRI with normal LV size, BNP is 89 pg/mL, and the abnormality is confined to the RV.
Postpartum and post-caesarean, but SpO2 98%, heart rate 88, no dyspnoea or chest pain, estimated PASP 24 mmHg without septal flattening, and the episodes coincide with NSVT on telemetry.

differential.diagnosis: Idiopathic right ventricular outflow tract ventricular tachycardia
differential.key_features: PVCs of LBBB morphology with inferior axis fit an RVOT focus, but the RV is structurally abnormal (dilated, dyskinetic, RVEF 39%) with V1-V3 T-wave inversion, which excludes the idiopathic form.
Sudden deaths in the family, but QTc is 452 ms (normal for a woman) and the heart is structurally abnormal on MRI, which CPVT is not.
Jerking lasted 8-15 seconds after pallor and sweating, with recovery within 30 seconds, no tongue bite and no post-ictal confusion: convulsive syncope, with NSVT captured on telemetry.

key_clinical_evidence: Two exertional collapses with pallor, sweating and brief jerks, palpitations for two weeks, and a father who died suddenly at 44: high-risk syncope despite the referral as postpartum seizures
Normal blood pressure, a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.18 and normal platelets and liver enzymes exclude pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
The ECG shows T-wave inversion in V1-V3 without RBBB and a possible epsilon wave; telemetry captures symptomatic NSVT and 4,832 PVCs of LBBB morphology
Cardiac MRI shows regional RV dyskinesia with RVEDVI 112 mL/m2 and RVEF 39%, a major Task Force criterion; with the V1-V3 T-wave inversion the diagnosis of ARVC is definite
LVEF 58-60% with normal LV size and BNP 89 pg/mL argue against peripartum cardiomyopathy
Management is an ICD, a breastfeeding-compatible beta-blocker, exercise restriction and family screening

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: a postpartum woman is referred with convulsive episodes presumed eclamptic. Normal blood pressure and urine and blood tests that exclude pre-eclampsia redirect attention to the heart. The resting ECG shows V1-V3 T-wave inversion and a possible epsilon wave; telemetry captures symptomatic NSVT, and cardiac MRI establishes ARVC. The father's sudden death at 44 is a pivotal clue that is easily dismissed in the postpartum setting.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Five required steps (ECG, targeted labs, TTE, telemetry, cardiac MRI); eclampsia, peripartum cardiomyopathy and epilepsy mimics; 3 red herrings; management spans ICD, a breastfeeding-compatible beta-blocker and family screening.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Priya Sharma is a 29-year-old woman, 10 days post-cesarean section, who presents to the emergency department via ambulance after two episodes of sudden loss of consciousness with witnessed convulsive movements today. The first episode occurred at approximately 10:00 AM while she was standing in the kitchen preparing a bottle of expressed breast milk for her newborn. Her husband, who was in the adjacent room, heard a crash and found her on the floor, unconscious, with her arms and legs stiffening and then jerking rhythmically for approximately 10-15 seconds. He describes her face as 'ghostly pale' and notes she was drenched in sweat just before the fall. She regained consciousness within approximately 20-30 seconds and was oriented within 1-2 minutes, though she felt lightheaded and nauseated. She had no recollection of the fall itself. She denied any preceding aura, visual disturbance, headache, or epigastric pain. She rested on the couch and felt well enough within 15 minutes to resume caring for the baby. The second episode occurred at approximately 3:30 PM while she was climbing the stairs to retrieve diapers from a closet. Her husband witnessed her suddenly stop mid-step, turn pale, and collapse backward. He caught her partially, preventing a significant fall. She again had brief jerking of all four limbs lasting approximately 8-10 seconds and was unresponsive during the episode. She recovered consciousness within 30 seconds and again returned to baseline rapidly. EMS was called and she was transported to the referring hospital where she was evaluated for suspected eclampsia given her recent pregnancy complicated by gestational hypertension. At the outside facility, blood pressure was 124/78 mmHg, she was afebrile, and a non-contrast CT of the head was unremarkable. Magnesium sulfate was initiated empirically and she was transferred to our tertiary center for further evaluation. Her husband emphasizes that both episodes seemed to occur during physical exertion — standing for a prolonged period and climbing stairs — and that she appeared very pale immediately before each collapse. She reports having felt occasional brief episodes of her 'heart racing' over the past two weeks but attributed them to anxiety about the new baby and postpartum hormonal changes. She denies headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, or peripheral edema beyond what she considers normal for her postpartum state.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration or oral trauma. No evidence of head injury. Husband reports patient's eyes 'rolled back' during the episode and she appeared pale and diaphoretic immediately before collapsing. Mild bilateral lower extremity edema, consistent with recent pregnancy. Well-healed cesarean incision without signs of infection.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-to-shin smooth bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive 3mm to 2mm. Fundoscopy: no papilledema, no hemorrhages. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus. CN V: Sensation intact in all divisions. Masseter strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal base and stride. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. Gait slightly guarded due to postoperative abdominal discomfort.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech fluent with normal rate and prosody. No dysarthria. Attention intact — serial 7s performed without error. Recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. No aphasia. No post-ictal confusion at the time of evaluation, approximately 4 hours after the most recent event. Mildly anxious but cooperative.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal, no rigidity or spasticity. Strength 5/5 in all major muscle groups bilaterally. No pronator drift. Mild tenderness at cesarean incision site on abdominal palpation, but no focal motor deficits.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No clonus. No hyperreflexia.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception intact in all four extremities. No sensory level. No dermatomal loss.
